findings.subject: carbimazole
findings.group: PTU dose in first trimester | mg
findings.correct: In pregnancy PTU is given at the lowest effective dose to keep FT4 in the upper half of the reference range, specialist-led (SPC; RCOG GTG76 2025). 200–400 mg/day is the general adult starting dose, not a pregnancy dose.

fixes.old: • T1 (<14 wks): PTU 200–400mg/day — carbimazole embryopathy risk in organogenesis
fixes.new: • T1 (<14 wks): PTU at the lowest effective dose, specialist-led (switch from carbimazole as early as possible, before 10 weeks) — carbimazole embryopathy risk in organogenesis

findings.note: The pregnancy bullet gives the non-pregnant adult starting range (200–400 mg/day) as the first-trimester dose. Over-treatment in pregnancy causes fetal hypothyroidism and goitre, and the SPC and RCOG say to use the lowest effective dose. The fix also adds RCOG's switch-before-10-weeks point. The 'around 20 weeks' switch back to carbimazole matches RCOG GTG76 2025 (as quoted by Wiles et al. 2025), so it is left unchanged.

findings.subject: anaemia in pregnancy
findings.correct: BSH 2020: Hb <110 g/L (T1) or <105 g/L (T2/T3) → oral iron and recheck in 2–3 weeks, under midwife/primary care. Refer to secondary care if Hb <70 g/L, significant symptoms, advanced gestation (>34 weeks) or no response.

fixes.old: • Pregnancy: Hb <110 g/L (1st trimester), <105 (later) → Same-day maternity; bleeding or compromise → 999
fixes.new: • Pregnancy: Hb <110 g/L (1st trimester), <105 (later) → start oral iron and inform the midwife; Hb <70 g/L, significant symptoms, rapid fall or late gestation (>34 weeks) → Same-day maternity; bleeding or compromise → 999

findings.note: Read literally, the one-page sends every pregnant woman whose Hb is below the anaemia threshold for same-day maternity assessment. That conflicts with BSH 2020 and with the site's own normocytic-anaemia and microcytosis pages, which escalate only severe, symptomatic, late or unresponsive anaemia.

findings.subject: magnesium

fixes.old: duration (risk appears after approximately 1 year)
fixes.new: duration (reported after as little as 3 months, most cases after about 1 year — MHRA)

findings.note: The current wording suggests there is no risk before 1 year. The MHRA says cases occur from 3 months.

findings.subject: neutrophils
findings.correct: Suspected neutropenic sepsis (unwell or febrile during/after systemic anticancer treatment) = IMMEDIATE referral/emergency assessment via the 24-hour acute oncology hotline or 999/A&E; antibiotics within 1 hour in hospital; do not wait for FBC (NICE CG151 1.2.1; NG253; UKONS triage uses ≥37.5°C)

fixes.old: Chemotherapy within 6 weeks with fever → Same-day neutropenic sepsis pathway.
fixes.new: Recent chemotherapy (within 6 weeks) with fever or feeling unwell → Immediate neutropenic sepsis pathway (acute oncology hotline / 999; do not wait for FBC).

fixes.old: • Neutropenic risk (chemotherapy within 6 weeks + fever) → Same-day
fixes.new: • Neutropenic risk (chemotherapy within 6 weeks + fever or unwell) → Immediate acute oncology hotline / 999

fixes.old: or on neutropenia-causing drugs → Same-day acute oncology; do not wait for FBC.
fixes.new: or on neutropenia-causing drugs → Immediate acute oncology hotline / 999; do not wait for FBC.

fixes.old: FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA: temperature ≥38°C or feeling unwell during chemotherapy = SAME-DAY oncology/haematology assessment (A&E if out of hours).
fixes.new: FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA: temperature ≥37.5°C or feeling unwell during chemotherapy = IMMEDIATE assessment via the 24-hour acute oncology/chemotherapy hotline (999/A&E if very unwell or the hotline cannot be reached).

findings.note: CG151 says refer suspected neutropenic sepsis immediately; 'same-day' understates a 1-hour-to-antibiotics emergency and conflicts with the site's own neutropenic-sepsis, leucopenia, pancytopenia and summaries/breast-cancer pages ('Immediately', 999/hotline, ≥37.5°C). The 6-week window is wider than NG253's 30 days, so it is safe and is kept. Search index JSON (assets/search/idx-pathway.json) may carry the old snippet; regenerate it rather than hand-editing.

findings.subject: neutrophils
findings.correct: NICE CG151: piperacillin with tazobactam monotherapy as initial empirical therapy; the BNF/SPC dose in neutropenic patients is 4.5 g IV every 6 hours (adjust for renal function); local protocol applies. UKONS's triage tool does not specify an antibiotic.

fixes.old: The UK Oncology Nursing Society (UKONS) neutropenic sepsis pathway specifies piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) 4.5 g IV every 8 hours as first-line in most centres.
fixes.new: NICE CG151 recommends piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) monotherapy as initial empirical treatment, given in hospital within 1 hour; the dose follows the hospital protocol and BNF (commonly 4.5 g IV every 6 hours in neutropenic patients, adjusted for renal function).

findings.note: Wrong frequency (every 8 h is the general-infection dose; the neutropenic dose is every 6 h) and wrong attribution (UKONS triage tool gives no antibiotic regimen; CG151 sets the drug choice). Hospital-only fact, but it is a dose statement.

fixes.new: oxygen saturation 95% or more

fixes.new: oxygen saturation 95% or more

findings.subject: children-pregnancy
findings.correct: Pre-eclampsia (not eclampsia): check BP and urine; any new hypertension (≥140/90) or proteinuria with headache → same-day maternity assessment (NICE NG133); ≥160/110, seizure or severe features → emergency (999)

fixes.old: Severe headache in pregnancy ≥20 weeks: eclampsia — BP check + 999 if ≥160/110
fixes.new: Severe headache in pregnancy ≥20 weeks: pre-eclampsia — check BP and urine; same-day maternity assessment if BP ≥140/90 or proteinuria (NG133); 999 if ≥160/110, seizure or severe features

findings.note: Mislabels pre-eclampsia as eclampsia and implies a woman with severe headache and BP 140–159/90–109 needs no urgent action. Other site pages (articles-data-3, pathways-redflags) already give same-day maternity wording.

findings.subject: children-pregnancy
findings.correct: MHRA DSU June 2023: avoid systemic NSAIDs from 20 weeks unless clinically necessary (oligohydramnios, fetal renal dysfunction); contraindicated from 28 weeks (premature closure of ductus arteriosus)

fixes.old: NSAIDs are contraindicated after 20 weeks (risk of premature closure of ductus arteriosus).
fixes.new: NSAIDs should be avoided from 20 weeks unless clinically necessary (oligohydramnios, fetal renal dysfunction) and are contraindicated from 28 weeks (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus) — MHRA 2023.

fixes.old: Do NOT prescribe NSAIDs in pregnancy (>20 weeks) or colchicine without specialist oversight.
fixes.new: Do NOT prescribe NSAIDs in pregnancy (avoid from 20 weeks, contraindicated from 28 weeks) or colchicine without specialist oversight.

findings.note: Gout page attributes the 20-week rule to ductus closure (a third-trimester/28-week risk) and calls it a contraindication; align with the MHRA wording already used on osteoarthritis and ankylosing-spondylitis pages. Other pages saying 'avoid NSAIDs from 20 weeks' are acceptable.

fixes.new: quetiapine (licensed add-on as quetiapine XL, 50 mg at bedtime titrated to 150–300 mg/day per SPC;

findings.subject: glucagon
findings.correct: GlucaGen 1 mg IM for adults and children >25 kg or older than 6–8 years; 0.5 mg for children <25 kg or younger than 6–8 years. Baqsimi 3 mg nasal licensed from age 4

fixes.old: Prescribe glucagon (GlucaGen HypoKit 1 mg IM or Baqsimi 3 mg nasal) in a quantity
fixes.new: Prescribe glucagon (GlucaGen HypoKit 1 mg IM — 0.5 mg if child under 25 kg or under 6–8 years; or Baqsimi 3 mg nasal, age 4+) in a quantity

findings.note: Missing weight/age band. Page is adult-focused (JBDS) but recommends kits at school and training teachers; add the paediatric band where prescribing is described. Other glucagon 1 mg statements are in adult contexts and are correct.

findings.subject: lithium
findings.correct: NICE CG185: level every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months (3-monthly if older, interacting drugs, renal/thyroid impairment, raised calcium, poor adherence or last level ≥0.8)

fixes.old: then every 3 months (6-monthly if very stable, per local protocol)
fixes.new: then every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months (stay 3-monthly if higher risk — NICE CG185)

findings.note: Aligns with tools/management/bipolar-lithium.html and shared-care-monitoring-data.js; the 6-monthly step is NICE, not local protocol.

findings.subject: aspirin
findings.correct: Resolved suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated (bleeding disorder, anticoagulant); no brain imaging needed first (NICE NG128). Ongoing deficit = stroke pathway, no aspirin before imaging.

fixes.old: Give aspirin 300mg now (if haemorrhage unlikely clinically and no CT available).
fixes.new: Give aspirin 300mg now unless contraindicated (NICE NG128: no brain imaging needed first for resolved suspected TIA; anticoagulated or bleeding disorder → specialist advice).

fixes.old: Do NOT give aspirin without excluding haemorrhage if clinically uncertain.
fixes.new: Do NOT give aspirin if symptoms are ongoing (stroke pathway: imaging first), or if anticoagulated or with a bleeding disorder, without specialist advice.

findings.note: The qualifier 'if haemorrhage unlikely clinically and no CT available' and 'do not give without excluding haemorrhage if uncertain' implies imaging gating for resolved TIA, contradicting NG128 and ~40 other statements on the site (including elsewhere on the same page). Risk: GP withholds the loading dose.

findings.subject: platelets
findings.correct: Routine platelet-count monitoring is not required in obstetric patients receiving LMWH only (BSH HIT guideline, Watson et al 2012; RCOG GTG37a). Monitor only if UFH was given first or per specialist plan.

fixes.old: Platelet count at baseline and monthly on LMWH.
fixes.new: Routine platelet monitoring is not needed on LMWH alone in pregnancy (BSH/RCOG); follow the specialist monitoring plan.

findings.note: Pregnancy item. Monthly platelet counts on LMWH alone are not UK guidance and push unnecessary monitoring into primary care.

findings.subject: platelets
findings.group: Liver disease — platelet threshold for portal hypertension
findings.correct: Baveno VII: in compensated advanced chronic liver disease, platelets ≤150 × 10⁹/L (or LSM ≥20 kPa) means variceal screening is needed; LSM <15 kPa with platelets ≥150 rules out CSPH. <100 is too low a trigger.

fixes.old: Platelets <100 × 10⁹/L = portal hypertension indicator → hepatology referral plus OGD for varices
fixes.new: Platelets ≤150 × 10⁹/L in suspected advanced liver disease = possible portal hypertension → hepatology referral; variceal screening (OGD) if platelets ≤150 or liver stiffness ≥20 kPa (Baveno VII)

findings.note: The <100 cut-off under-triggers referral and screening for varices. Low clinical-severity error, but the threshold is wrong.

findings.subject: metronidazole
findings.correct: Metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel is a first-line option for BV only. It is not effective for Trichomonas vaginalis, which needs systemic (oral) metronidazole 400–500 mg BD for 7 days (BASHH TV 2021).

fixes.old: ✓ First-line for BV and trichomonas
fixes.new: ✓ First-line for BV (oral or vaginal gel) and trichomonas (oral only — vaginal gel is not effective for TV)

findings.note: The drug card is headed 'Metronidazole (oral / vaginal gel)' and its badge says 'First-line for BV and trichomonas'. Read that way, it implies the gel treats TV. Intravaginal metronidazole does not reach therapeutic levels in the urethra or periurethral glands, so BASHH recommends oral treatment only. The dose line on the same card already gives TV as oral 400–500 mg BD for 7 days, so this changes only the badge wording. Grep found this one occurrence on the site.

findings.subject: morphine
findings.correct: eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m² is CKD category G4 (15–29), not G3b (30–44). The opioid teaching point (avoid morphine, eGFR <30) stays correct.

fixes.old: Mrs. Patel’s eGFR 28 is confirmed CKD 3b:
fixes.new: Mrs. Patel’s eGFR 28 is CKD G4 (eGFR 15–29):

fixes.old: Mrs. Patel’s eGFR 28 = CKD 3b;
fixes.new: Mrs. Patel’s eGFR 28 = CKD G4;

fixes.old: eGFR 28 — CKD 3b — CRITICAL for opioid choice
fixes.new: eGFR 28 — CKD G4 — CRITICAL for opioid choice

findings.note: Three places in the palliative case label eGFR 28 as CKD 3b. It is G4. The renal-opioid advice (avoid morphine below eGFR 30; specialist advice; oxycodone/alfentanil) is unaffected. The first fix also drops 'confirmed', because a single eGFR from 3 weeks ago in a vomiting, dehydrated patient does not confirm a CKD stage (the same sentence goes on to suggest a pre-renal element). Grep found no other site file that stages eGFR 28 as 3b.

findings.subject: glucose
findings.group: suspected type 1 diabetes in a child (secondary enuresis)
findings.correct: In a child with polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss, a random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (not >11.1) supports diabetes, and a capillary reading is not by itself a formal diagnosis. NICE NG18 says refer immediately (same day) to the paediatric diabetes team and do not wait for confirmatory tests.
findings.source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng18 (rec 1.1.1–1.1.2: suspected T1D → same-day referral to multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team); WHO diagnostic threshold random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms

fixes.old: Random glucose >11.1 mmol/L = diabetes diagnosis.
fixes.new: A random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more with these symptoms strongly suggests diabetes; do not wait for confirmatory tests: refer the same day to the paediatric diabetes team (NICE NG18).

findings.note: The threshold sign is wrong (> instead of ≥). Calling a capillary reading a 'diagnosis' could also encourage the GP to confirm it in primary care before referring, which NG18 advises against. The adjacent cell ('>11.1 → same-day paediatric diabetes team') is acceptable in context.

findings.subject: glucose
findings.correct: Endocrine Society (Cryer 2009) criteria: plasma glucose <3.0 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) with insulin ≥3 µU/mL (≥18 pmol/L), C-peptide ≥0.6 ng/mL (≥0.2 nmol/L) and proinsulin ≥5 pmol/L. <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) is an older criterion.
findings.source: https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/94/3/709/2596186 (Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycemic disorders, 2009)

fixes.old: (blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L)
fixes.new: (plasma glucose <3.0 mmol/L)

findings.note: The insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin cut-offs in the same sentence already match the Endocrine Society criteria. Only the glucose threshold is out of date. This is a secondary-care teaching point, so it is low priority.
